**THINGS** located near rivers are less evident in distant places than those that are remote from such rivers and marshes.

**AMONG** things of equal thickness, those that are closer to the eye will appear more sparse, and those more remote will appear denser.

**THE EYE** that has a larger pupil will see the object as a larger figure. This is demonstrated by looking at a celestial body <note>original: "corpo celeste"; likely referring to the sun or moon</note> through a tiny hole <term>spiracolo: a small aperture or pinhole</term> made with a needle in paper; because only a small part of its light can operate, that body seems to diminish in size by as much as the portion of light seeing it is lacking from its whole.

**THE AIR** that is thickened and interposed between the eye and the object renders the boundaries of that object uncertain and confused, and makes the object appear larger than it is. This happens because linear perspective <term>prospettiva lineare: the mathematical system of creating depth through converging lines</term> does not diminish the angle that carries its images to the eye, but the perspective of colors <term>prospettiva de' colori: also known as aerial perspective, where color and clarity change with distance</term> pushes and removes it to a greater distance than it actually is; thus, one removes it from the eye, and the other preserves its magnitude.

**WHEN** the sun is in the west, the falling mists thicken the air, and things not seen by the sun remain dark and confused, while those illuminated by the sun turn reddish and yellowish, according to how the sun appears on the horizon. Furthermore, the things illuminated by this light are very evident, especially the buildings and houses of cities and villas, because their shadows are dark; it seems that their clear appearance arises from confused and uncertain backgrounds, because everything is of one color unless it is seen by the sun.

**AN OBJECT** illuminated by the sun is also illuminated by the air, so that two shadows are created; of these, the one that has its central line pointing directly to the center of the sun will be darker. The central line of the primary and derivative light will always be aligned with the central line of the primary or derivative shadows. <note>Leonardo distinguishes between "primary" shadows on the object itself and "derivative" shadows cast onto other surfaces.</note>

**THE SUN** makes a beautiful spectacle when it is in the west, illuminating all the high buildings of cities and castles, and the tall trees of the countryside, tinting them with its color. Everything else from there downwards remains with little relief, because being illuminated only by the air, there is little difference between the shadows and the lights, and for this reason, they do not stand out much. Those things that rise highest among them are touched by the solar rays and, as has been said, are tinted in their color; therefore, you must take the color with which you make your sun, and mix it into whatever light color you use to illuminate those bodies.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the "Path of Departure" (Utkrānti), specifically addressing whether the process of the soul's exit from the body differs between the spiritually enlightened person and the unenlightened person.</meta>

Regarding the sensory organs such as speech, at the time when the soul desires to move into another body <note>the transition between incarnations</note>, another scriptural passage—beginning with the question, "Where then does this person stay?"—describes action as the primary support:
- "What they spoke of was action <note>original: "karma"</note>; what they praised was action." 
In response to this, it is said: in that context, the role of action is described as the driving force behind the bondage of the senses and their objects <term>graha and atigraha; a Vedic classification of the sensory organs and the external objects that 'seize' them</term>. In the present discussion, however, we speak of the soul resting upon the subtle elements <note>original: "bhūta"</note> to produce a new body. Even though the word "praise" is used for action, it only highlights the primary importance of action in determining the *type* of rebirth; it does not exclude the physical elements as a necessary support. Therefore, there is no contradiction between these teachings.

# **And [the departure is] the same until the beginning of the path; and the immortality [attained] is without burning [the bonds]. (4.2.7)**

## **Section on the Start of the Path (4.2.7)**

Does this departure <note>original: "utkrānti"</note> happen in the same way for both the wise and the ignorant, or is there a difference? Those who are in doubt might argue that there is a difference. They might say that because this departure involves taking support from the elements for the sake of rebirth, and because the wise person does not undergo rebirth—having already attained immortality—this process must only apply to the ignorant. 

If one objects that this process is described within the context of the "Science of Knowledge" <note>the Vidya-prakarana, or sections of the Upanishads dealing with meditation and realization</note> and thus must apply only to the wise, we reply: No. It is like the descriptions of sleep or hunger. When the scripture says, "When a person is said to be 'sleeping'" or "is 'hungry'" or "is 'thirsty,'" it is describing natural states common to all living beings. These are mentioned in the teachings on knowledge only to help explain the ultimate nature of the Self—to show how the light <note>original: "tejas"</note> of a dying person merges into the Supreme Deity to illustrate the truth: "That Thou Art." It is not meant to suggest that the wise experience a unique physical departure. Furthermore, the scripture explicitly states for the Knower: "his vital breaths do not depart." Therefore, this general process of departure applies to the ignorant as well.

This being the case, we conclude: This departure, beginning with the merging of "speech into the mind," is common to both the wise and the ignorant until they reach the "start of the path" <note>the point where the soul enters a specific channel or vein to exit the body</note>. Up to this point, there is no audible difference in the process. The ignorant person, driven by karma, rests upon the subtle elements that serve as the "seed" for a new body and continues in the cycle of rebirth. The wise person, however, follows the path through the "gate of the heart" <note>the Sushumna vein</note> illuminated by knowledge. 

As for the "immortality" mentioned as being attained by the wise: this refers to a relative immortality <note>original: "āpekṣikam-amṛtatvam"</note> achieved through lower forms of meditation, without yet having completely "burnt" <note>destroyed</note> the afflictions of ignorance. In such a state, a departure and a path are still possible. Because the vital breaths cannot move without a physical support, the soul still relies on the subtle elements. Thus, there is no error in this view.

# **That [remains] until the attainment [of liberation], because of the declaration of worldly existence. (4.2.8)**

## **Section on the Description of Worldly Existence (4.2.8)**

When the scripture says "the light merges into the Supreme Deity," it means that the light—accompanied by the individual soul, the vital breaths, the senses, and the other elements—merges into the Divine. One might ask: what kind of "merging" is this? Some might argue it is an absolute dissolution of the individual's nature, as the Supreme Deity is the source of all things. 

To this, we reply: that subtle light and the other elements that support the senses remain until the final attainment of liberation <term>saṃsāra; the cycle of death and rebirth</term> through perfect knowledge. We know this because the scriptures continue to describe the soul's transmigrations: "Some souls enter a womb for a body, others follow after stationary things <note>such as plants</note> according to their actions and their knowledge." 

If every soul underwent a total dissolution into the Divine at the moment of death, then everyone would attain the Absolute <note>original: "Brahman"</note> regardless of their wisdom, making all spiritual instructions and the science of knowledge useless. Bondage caused by false knowledge cannot be severed without right knowledge. Therefore, even though the soul "merges" into the Divine at death, it is like the merging that happens in deep sleep or a general cosmic dissolution—the "seed" of potential existence remains.

# **And [it is] subtle in size, and is perceived as such. (4.2.9)**

## **(4.2.9)**

That light, joined with the other elements, which serves as the support for the individual soul <note>original: "jīva"</note> as it departs from this body, must be subtle in its essential nature and its size. This is confirmed by the fact that it is not perceived by onlookers as it exits the body.

<summary>This page discusses the process of the soul's departure (Utkrānti) from the body, arguing that the initial stages are identical for both the enlightened and the ignorant. It clarifies that the subtle body remains intact until final liberation, acting as a "seed" for future existence unless destroyed by perfect knowledge.</summary>

LIII. In the controversy regarding whether the transmutation of baser things into more precious ones can occur naturally through the art of alchemy, and therefore whether gold can be made from a baser metal, it seems one must argue that there is no effective reason to show the production of gold is entirely impossible. Although it is considered extremely difficult, it is not repugnant in terms of matter, which is suitable to be altered and led to the form of gold, nor in terms of method, which is through the natural cooking <note>original: "decoctionem"</note> of fire. Although perhaps more things are required than human industry can supply so that a mixed body might exist and coagulate from earth and water, or from exhalation and vapor—and therefore the substance of gold cannot be perfected in the veins of caverns from the dust of the earth and the liquid of water solely by heat, but cold and dryness are also required—nevertheless, fewer things are required to produce another mixture differing in perfection from a mixture that has already coagulated and exists. Consequently, where a metal has already coalesced into the substance of a metal, fire alone will be able to supply what is necessary to perfect and change that metal into another. This is most true if the metals do not differ in species, as Albertus Magnus teaches in Book 3, On Metals, tractate 1, chapter 7, following Callisthenes.

LIV. Therefore, it seems far more probable that alchemy can achieve its goal and transmute other metals into gold by fire than that it cannot. For since, by the industry of human art, certain animals can be generated from inanimate bodies, such as bees from the fresh bellies of slaughtered oxen buried only in dung, why can more excellent metals (which are, generally speaking, inanimate) not also be produced from baser ones? Especially since it is believed that a certain seed, as it were, of gold resides within baser metals, implanted in them naturally—that is, by reason of their generic or specific nature—which seed, having been in some way impressed by the influx of the heavens, is nurtured by heat and grows into gold. Furthermore, although the art of producing gold does not seem to be prohibited by any law in the public forum, such that it is not permitted to practice it here and there, nevertheless, it is deservedly judged illicit and pernicious at least by reason of the circumstances; that is, the end, the manner, the person, and the time. Gregory of Valencia, volume 3, disputation 6, question 13, part 2, and Delrio agrees at the end of book 1 when he says that in the forum of the conscience <note>original: "in foro poli"</note> it should not be permitted indiscriminately, but with discretion; indeed, for most people, it should be considered as pernicious as it is illicit.

<header>### Gem of Lofty Wisdom in the Word of Moses</header>

The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, used to go out into the rain when it fell and uncover his head to it so that it would touch him. He would say: "It has newly come from its Lord." Look at this knowledge of God from this Prophet; how majestic, high, and clear it is! The rain subjugated the best of humanity because of its proximity to its Lord. It was like the Messenger to whom revelation descends. It called him through its state and essence, so he went out to it to receive the divine benefit it brought from his Lord. Had he not obtained a divine benefit from it touching him, he would not have gone out to it. This is the message of the water from which God made "every living thing" <note>Quran 21:30</note>. Understand this.

As for the wisdom of him being placed in the ark and cast into the river, the ark represents his <term>nasut</term> <gloss>human nature or physical body</gloss>. The river <note>original: "al-yamm"</note> represents the knowledge he obtained by means of this body. This includes what was given to him by the faculties of theoretical thought, the senses, and the imagination. None of these, nor their like, would exist for this human soul without the existence of this elemental body. 

When the soul entered this body and was commanded to manage and direct it, God made these faculties tools to reach what God intended for it in the management of this ark, within which lies the tranquility of the Lord. He was cast into the river so that he might obtain the various branches of knowledge through these faculties. Through this, He informed him that even though the spirit managing him is the king, it can only manage him through these faculties. He accompanied him with these powers existing in this human nature, which was expressed as the "ark" in the language of symbols and wisdom.

Similarly, the management of the Truth <note>original: "al-Haqq"</note> over the world is only done through the world, or through its image. He only manages it through itself, just as a child depends on the existence of a parent, effects depend on their causes, conditions on their prerequisites, results on their premises, and proofs on their evidence. All of this is part of the world, and it is the management of the Truth within it. He only manages it through it. 

When we say "or through its image," meaning the image of the world, I mean the Beautiful Names and Lofty Attributes by which the Truth named Himself and with which He is described. Every name by which He is called has a meaning and a spirit that we find within the world. Therefore, the world is also managed only through the image of the world.

For this reason, He said regarding the creation of Adam, who is the comprehensive program of the descriptions of the Divine Presence—which are the Essence, Attributes, and Acts: "God created Adam in His image." His image is nothing other than the Divine Presence. He placed within this noble summary, which is the Perfect Human <note>original: "al-Insan al-Kamil"</note>, all the divine names and the realities of everything that exists outside him in the great, separate world. He made him a spirit...
